1:
The Gadarenes had begged Jesus to leave their coasts, and Gill and Henry read the crossing as his taking them at their word. Henry finds justice in the departure, since Christ does not tarry where he is unwelcome, and patience in it, since no destroying judgment was left behind; no return visit is ever recorded, and Gadara was among the first towns besieged when the Roman wars began soon after.

Which city he came to draws the most comment. Chrysostom distributes the towns: Bethlehem received him to be born, Nazareth brought him up, Capernaum had him continually inhabiting it. Barnes, Clarke, Robertson and Calvin read Capernaum, and Ellicott adds that it became his own city after the departure from Nazareth, which is never so described. Jerome dissents, allowing that the city may be Nazareth, whence he was called a Nazarene. Augustine offers a harmonising alternative: all Galilee might be called Christ's city, as the whole Roman empire was still called the Roman city, and Capernaum had been exalted into the metropolis of Galilee. On that reading Matthew has passed over everything between the entry into Galilee and the arrival, as the evangelists often carry the thread forward without noticing an interval. Ellicott concedes the harmonist is baffled here; Clarke goes further and says the verse properly belongs to the preceding chapter.

The bringing is filled out from the parallels. Gill counts four bearers, following Mark. Ellicott gathers that Jesus taught in a house with courtyard and gateway packed, and that Pharisees and doctors of the law had come from every village of Galilee and Judaea and also from Jerusalem, which he treats as one of the few traces of an unrecorded ministry there. Barnes spends his longest passage on architecture, since the uncovering of the roof puzzles western readers: the eastern house is square and single-storied, its central court open above and shaded in heat or wet by an awning stretched on cords. Rolling that awning back is what Mark means by uncovering the roof, and the railing round the court is Luke's tiling. Chrysostom separates this man from the paralytic of John, who lay by the pool thirty-eight years with nobody to help him.

Whose faith Jesus saw is the passage's real question. Jerome says flatly that it was not the sick man's but that of those who bore him, and Chrysologus marvels that another's belief availed to heal a man within and without, adding that a physician does not consult the wishes of the patient when the malady requires otherwise. Chrysostom allows both, observing that the man would hardly have let himself be lowered through a roof without conviction of his own. Calvin turns it into a general enquiry into how far one profits by the faith of others, and answers by degrees: Abraham's faith reached his seed, and grace extends to believers' children before birth; for adults who have none, another's faith works only indirectly, through prayer, and they reach salvation only when made partakers of the same faith. Reconciliation, he insists, comes no other way, so the paralytic must have believed.

The word spoken is tender. Jerome exclaims at the humility of it, that a man despised and crippled in every limb, whom the priests would not deign to touch, is addressed as son. Ellicott prefers child, hearing either comparative youth or a fatherly tone, and insists the English misleads, since the Greek is indicative and reports a pardon already granted rather than wishing for one. Clarke reports the rabbinic maxim that no diseased person could be healed until his sins were blotted out, grounding it in the psalm that joins forgiving iniquity to healing disease. Calvin sees Christ granting something other than what was asked because he begins at the cause: men feel the affliction and not the sin, and seek relief from present pain as a sick man might ignore the disease behind it.
3:
The charge of blasphemy is granted force by the very commentators who reject it. Barnes traces the word from speaking evil of anyone to its religious use, attempting what belongs to God alone, and says the scribes reasoned correctly that none can forgive sins but God: no prophet had this power, so Jesus was understood to affirm that he was divine. Ellicott hears an echo of the accusation already laid at Jerusalem, that he made himself equal with God, and thinks some of the same objectors may be present; what they failed to weigh was that God might delegate the power to chosen servants, or that the Teacher might himself be one with God. Calvin is harsher: if they thought the words blameworthy, why not ask him to explain, and why take in a bad sense language the prophets often use of God's grace? They keep silent, he says, to slander him among their own class when absent. Clarke adds that the scribes were the learned of their time, and that knowledge not held in dependence on God only blinds.

That he answered thoughts nobody had spoken is treated by Gill, Barnes and Clarke as the first proof, since searching the heart belongs to God alone; Jerome said the same, that in seeing their thoughts he shewed himself God, who alone knows the heart. Ellicott notes the better manuscripts read seeing rather than knowing, an immediate act of intuition.

On the comparison of the two sayings the voices diverge instructively. Clarke holds them equally easy and equally difficult, since both require unlimited power, and adds a punctuation note: the comma belongs after easier. Ellicott argues the other way: the pardon was easier to utter because no outward test could touch it, while the command to rise risked immediate and visible failure. Chrysostom set it out plainly: by as much as the soul is better than the body, forgiving sin is the greater work, but because one can be seen and the other cannot, he does the lesser and more evident miracle to prove the greater. Calvin agrees that Christ adapts himself to their capacity, being carnal men more moved by outward signs.

The interrupted sentence at the centre is noticed from two directions. The Gloss observes that the clause may belong to Christ or the Evangelist, and that if it is Christ's the sentence is left imperfect, the action supplying the missing consequent. Robertson notices the same seam differently: the narrator's words stand oddly inside a saying, Mark has them in precisely the same place, and this is one of many signs both later Gospels used Mark. Ellicott renders the disputed noun authority rather than power, ties it to the discourse in John where authority to judge is given because he is the Son of Man, and hears in the command to take up the bed the syllables spoken at Bethesda, meant to recall what the Jerusalem scribes had seen. Clarke counts three miracles in the episode: the remission, the discernment, and the cure. Calvin marks the difference from what apostles and pastors exercise, who declare a pardon entrusted to them rather than grant one, and reads on earth to mean forgiveness is not sought at a distance.

The crowd's response is textually contested. Clarke reports manuscripts reading feared where the received text has wondered, the Gothic and one Itala copy conjoining both; Ellicott judges fear the better reading, matching Mark's amazement and Luke's fear, and preserves their sayings, that they never saw it after this fashion and had seen strange things that day. Barnes cautions that their words about power given to men record the crowd's feelings, not the evangelist's account of Christ's nature, and Calvin and Ellicott both find the confession half right: human nature was indeed honoured, but they stopped at delegated authority without perceiving the majesty of God united to flesh.
9:
The two names are the first business. Jerome observes that the other evangelists, out of respect, call him Levi, while this Gospel gives both name and trade, on the principle that the righteous man accuses himself, so no reader need despair who turns to better things. Barnes finds the same reticence elsewhere: Luke records that he left all, which said of himself would have been self-praise. Ellicott suggests a new name superseding an old one, as with Simon called Peter, made likelier by its meaning, the gift of God, set beside Theodore and Dorotheus; Clarke derives it from a Syriac word for a gift, and Calvin thinks Levi was the name his countrymen used, the foreign one taken with the office.

The office is described with unusual precision. Robertson places the custom-house at Capernaum, taking toll from boats crossing outside Herod's territory and from the Damascus caravan route, and explains the contempt for publicans by their reputation for graft, recalling that even a proconsul of Syria was accused by Cicero of relieving Jews and Syrians of legitimate taxes for money. Ellicott calls it the douane of the lake, a levy on the fish and fruit passing through the port. Lightfoot puts him by the sea, gathering rates from those who sailed across, preserves a rabbinic sabbath ruling about a publican's note of remitted duty, and relays a Talmudic tradition naming five disciples of Jesus, one called Mathai. Calvin says only that the trade was noted for plundering and then particularly infamous.

Why the call came so late is Chrysostom's question, answered twice in the same terms: Matthew was not summoned with Peter and John because he was still hardened, and only after many miracles and much fame did the one who knows the secrets of each mind judge him ready. He draws two further lessons: that Christ withdrew after the healing rather than provoke envy, which we should imitate, and that the evangelist shows self-denial in not disguising his former life. The Gloss, citing Anselm, says the call stands among the miracles because a publican becoming an Apostle was one. Jerome answers pagan critics, the Emperor Julian among them, who argue that either the historian lies or the followers were reckless: they forget the signs already done, and the brightness of the hidden Godhead in his face; if a loadstone draws iron, how much more the Lord of creation.

The obedience is read as evidence. Clarke reflects on how much is lost by delay; Calvin sees the divine power of Christ's word, since not all who hear are equally moved, and takes this for a set example that the calling was not from man. Henry notes that Christ found him at work, as Satan comes to the idle; that he was not seeking Christ but was spoken to first; and that while the fishermen are found fishing again later, he never sits at the receipt of custom again.

Gill, Clarke, Barnes, Ellicott, Wesley and Henry all supply from Luke the great feast this Gospel reduces to sitting at meat in the house; Barnes and Ellicott read deliberate humility in the omission, and Ellicott takes it for a farewell entertainment before the new calling began. The Gloss finds an omen in it, that the future teacher of the Gentiles at his own conversion drew a crowd of sinners after him, doing by example what he would soon do by word. Clarke holds the word rendered sinners generally means heathens through the Gospels, and the Gloss reports Tertullian arguing so from the saying that there should be no payer of tribute in Israel, which would make Matthew no Jew; the Gloss rejects it, since the Lord took care not to breach the Law by eating with Gentiles, and Ellicott allows Gentiles may have been present without the term designating them. Robertson calls the party a strange medley.
11:
The complaint is put obliquely. Ellicott has the scribes of the Pharisees, probably the same men present at the healing, declining to enter a publican's house and watching the guests from outside, and counts two questions, one to the disciples and one about their Master. Calvin reads an attempt to detach the disciples by reproaching them with something at first sight shameful, and credits them with carrying the calumny to Christ rather than answering it themselves. Barnes explains why the charge bit: eating with a man signals intimacy, so the inference was that he could not himself be righteous. Clarke turns it inward: whoever never felt himself indebted to mercy is rarely concerned for anyone else's salvation.

The reply is a proverb Clarke says none could misapply. Ellicott renders the first term they that are strong, notes Luke's more clinical they that are in health, and hears grave irony: those addressed suffered the worst spiritual disease while reckoning themselves without spot, and are answered on their own valuation, so by their own showing they cannot object to the physician working where need is greatest.

Calvin builds his longest passage on two errors: the scribes left the office of Christ out of account, and spared their own vices while despising everyone else's. He calls the concession to their righteousness an admission made in irony, then sets out the office itself, to quicken the dead, justify the condemned, wash the polluted, and clothe with glory those covered in shame; if that was the reason for the flesh and the blood, no one should think it strange that the worst of men are gathered in. The application is meant to sting: those who feel a stain in being joined by Baptism and the Lord's Supper to vile men should search their own evils without flattery. Rabanus takes the image further: the physician healed by a strange medicine, being wounded for our iniquities; the whole are those establishing their own righteousness, the sick those who, seeing the Law cannot justify, submit in penitence. Augustine guards against misreading: sinners are not loved because they are sinners, the physician calling the sick to be saved from iniquity as from a sickness, and that by repentance.

On the prophetic text there is a plain disagreement about its source. Barnes, Ellicott, Calvin and Wesley cite Hosea; Clarke gives the words instead to Samuel's rebuke of Saul, and the majority should be followed. Barnes insists the saying is no repudiation of sacrifice, which God commanded, but a Hebrew idiom preferring mercy to it, and observes that sacrifice, the principal part of Jewish worship, stands here for external religion at large. Gill agrees the words are comparative, since offerings made in faith were acceptable, and identifies go and learn as a rabbinic formula for opening a passage, so Christ answers in their own dialect while reproving their ignorance. Clarke reports the same formula, preserves an older English rendering of mild-heartedness rather than mercy, and notes that the closing phrase unto repentance is absent from many manuscripts and versions and was dropped by Griesbach. Ellicott suspects the scribes were meant to read the context too, finding their own likeness in goodness that is as a morning cloud.

Who the righteous are is left deliberately open. Chrysostom hears irony again: the saying does not run mercy as well as sacrifice but chooses one and rejects the other, and none on earth is righteous. Hilary presses the difficulty: if Christ came for all, were there some for whom he need not come? No man, he answers, is righteous by the law. The Gloss offers both readings, the feignedly righteous who boasted of it, or genuinely upright men such as Nathanael and the Baptist who needed no call to repentance. Calvin ends where the objection began: pardon is given not to cherish sins but to recall us to a devout life.
14:
Who asked is disputed by the sources themselves. Matthew names the Baptist's disciples, Luke the Pharisees, Mark seems to join both; Augustine reconciles them by putting John's disciples among the guests, all pressing one objection. Chrysostom notices they name themselves first and the Pharisees second to add weight, and thinks the Pharisees brought them along as they later brought the Herodians. Calvin sees a stratagem to draw them into the Pharisees' party, warning that cunning men divide us over trifles, and that almost everyone overvalues outward rudiments and makes his own practice a law for others. Robertson and Barnes look to the prison: John languished there, his followers fasting in grief, and they may have blamed Jesus for doing nothing. Ellicott adds that the Baptist's followers remained a distinct body with their own fasts and prayers, and that being no hypocrites they are answered without the sternness used on their companions.

The customs behind the question get close attention. Barnes notes the twice-weekly fast beyond the national days, so established that John did not think himself authorised to alter it. Lightfoot traces the choice of the second and fifth days to a tradition of ten decrees of Ezra appointing public reading of the law then, explained in turn from Moses going up for the second tables on the fifth day and coming down appeased on the second. Both he and Clarke report fasts for stranger ends, to procure a lucky dream, obtain its interpretation, or turn aside its ill import, Clarke citing a whole tract of them. Henry observes the boast was unverifiable anyway, since Christ had told his disciples to keep their fasts private, so their religion could not be judged by what the world saw.

The answer changes the image. Chrysostom points out that he had just called himself Physician and now Bridegroom, recalling the Baptist's saying that he who has the bride is the bridegroom; Jerome makes Christ the Bridegroom and the Church the Bride, of whose union the Apostles were born, so they cannot mourn while he is in the chamber. Ellicott presses hardest, arguing the words would startle the questioners by making the meal in Matthew's house a wedding-feast, the disciples guests singly and the bride collectively. Calvin will not object to deriving the figure from the Baptist but doubts it rests on solid grounds, preferring that Christ simply spares his disciples while with them. On the phrase itself Lightfoot, Clarke, Robertson and Calvin agree it means the wedding guests, and Lightfoot preserves the custom of breaking a costly glass before over-merry guests, since a man may not fill his mouth with laughter in this world.

Augustine distinguishes two kinds of fasting, one humbling the soul with groaning and bodily chastisement, another suspending carnal desire by the joy of spiritual meditation, and finds both answered here, the first by the saying about mourning, the second by the comparisons that follow; that this Gospel writes mourn where the others write fast tells him which is meant.

On the fasting to come the readings diverge. Ellicott denies the words impose an obligation while granting they sanction the principle, and thinks they favour fasts at seasons of sorrow over frequent fixed ones; he also marks this the first plain hint of the death in the public teaching. Clarke reconstructs a different history: the earliest annual fast commemorated not forty days in the wilderness but the forty hours Christ lay under death, the churches kept it variously for days or whole weeks, and calling all of them a forty days' fast came of putting days where hours belonged. Jerome reports that Montanus, Prisca and Maximilla built a forty days' abstinence after Pentecost on this text, against the Church's practice of reaching the passion through humiliation of the flesh. Hilary reads the withdrawal spiritually: those who do not believe Christ risen go without the food of life.
16:
The commentators agree about the philology before they divide about the meaning. Clarke, Robertson, Barnes and Wesley all explain that the cloth is unfulled, not yet through the fuller's hands, so it shrinks when wet and drags away the sound cloth it was sewn to; Clarke gives the Greek and an old Latin reading that the patch takes away the garment's fullness. On the vessels there is the same unanimity: not glass but skins, whole hides of goat or sheep. Barnes explains why the East used them, since caravans crossing sand could carry no glass or kegs, and reports a traveller's ox-skin bottle holding sixty gallons, two of which loaded a camel. Robertson adds that Spanish wine still comes to market in skins.

What the old garment and old skins stand for is contested, and both sides name each other. Jerome takes them for the Scribes and Pharisees, with the new cloth and new wine as Gospel precepts the Jews could not bear, and finds the Galatians attempting the same mixture of Law with Gospel. Gill defends that reading and attacks the alternative: the disciples were young converts renewed by the Spirit and clothed in Christ's righteousness, so they can hardly be called old garments and old bottles, nor is a severe discipline of fasting well figured by new wine, which usually stands for something pleasant. Calvin says flatly that those who compare the worn garments and decayed bottles to the Pharisees have no probability on their side, and meets the objection: calling the disciples old means not that they were wasted by long use but that they wanted strength. Chrysostom, Remigius and Clarke stand with him, Remigius identifying the new cloth with the grace of which fasting is one part and the new wine with the fulness of the Spirit the disciples could not then hold, though after the resurrection they became new skins and were said to be full of new wine.

Read that way the passage becomes a rule about pace. Chrysostom draws it out: the disciples were not yet renewed by the Spirit, no burden of precepts should be laid on men in that state, and there is a standing instruction to receive converts from the whole world leniently. The Gloss makes the same point from the other end: a heavy load laid on the untrained destroys the good already in him, and men soon to be filled with newness of grace ought not to be bound to the old observances. Calvin generalises: none are to be compelled indiscriminately to live alike, since natures differ and nothing suits everyone, and the weak must be spared lest violence break them. Clarke warns preachers that imposing mortifications not necessary to salvation before grace has prepared the heart is asking a child to do a man's work, and many auspicious beginnings have been ruined by haste. Hilary puts it darkly, that neither soul nor body, weakened by inveteracy of sin, can yet bear the sacraments of the new grace; Rabanus reads the figures as outer and inner, the garment our works abroad, the wine the faith and charity that renew within.

Ellicott alone follows the parables into later history. He notices the three comparisons hang together, wedding, garment, and the wine belonging to its joy, and guesses the guests' worn clothes made the figure vivid. The garment for him is the outward life, the wine the inward gifts, and the mistake is one the Church has repeated: sacramental ordinances, monastic vows, Puritan formulas and Quaker conventions engrafted on lives still barbarous or worldly, and, for the wine, Montanism, early Quakerism, and the body founded out of Edward Irving's history. The better way, he concludes, is Christ's, to keep the old garment and transform it from within, thread by thread. He notes too what Luke adds, that no one having drunk old wine wants new, saying the old is better.
18:
Lightfoot and Clarke distinguish two synagogue functionaries: the overseer, who is the minister and hands over the book of the law, and the ruler, who appoints who shall read the prophet, recite the phylacteries, and pass before the ark. Jairus held the second office, probably at Capernaum. Chrysostom stresses that the petitioner's rank was itself an embarrassment to the Pharisees, and adds that the girl was an only child of twelve. Henry puts the question the Gospel elsewhere asks, whether any of the rulers believed, and answers that here was one whose faith condemned the rest.

The chief difficulty is that this Gospel has the father say his daughter is already dead, while Mark and Luke have her dying and the news brought later on the road. Barnes, Clarke and Robertson resolve it grammatically, since the phrase need mean no more than that she was dying or must by now have died, Clarke reporting a conjecture that an underlying Hebrew form could be pointed either way. Augustine answers by intention rather than idiom: the father had so despaired that he was asking for her to be called back to life, and this Gospel gives what he wished and thought while the others give his words. From that he draws a rule: attend in anyone's speech not to the words but to the meaning they serve, since no one reports falsely who renders a man's sense in words he did not use. Chrysostom reads the phrase as either a guess from the length of the journey or the usual exaggeration of petitioners, who heighten their troubles to move those they beseech. Calvin refuses to make two stories of it, since so many circumstances converge that it is like three fingers pointing at one object.

Where the episode sits is a second dispute. Augustine notes that Mark and Luke place it just after the crossing back from the Gerasenes without fixing how long after, and that without some interval the feast in Matthew's house cannot be fitted in. Ellicott admits the sequence here looks unmistakable though the other two put many events between, and decides for this Gospel's order because its author was present while the others wrote at second hand.

The request itself is judged severely by some, generously by others. Chrysostom calls it dullness, that he asks two things, the presence and the laying on of the hand, exactly as the Syrian Naaman expected the prophet to come out and lay his hand on him; men dull of temper need sensible things, and the demand shows he had left her still breathing. Calvin makes the comparison that stings most, setting this ruler beside the centurion and finding the full brightness of faith in the heathen soldier and scarcely a spark in the officer of the synagogue, who ties the cure to a touch and trembles at the news of death; yet Christ yields to his prayer, so weak faith is no reason to stay away from praying. Calvin adds that the worship offered was the respect due a prophet, not divine honour. Gill remarks on what Christ passed over: the weakness of supposing he must come in person and by a prescribed method when he could have restored her absent.

The rising to follow draws its own comment. Remigius bids us imitate a mercy that rose the moment it was asked, and finds a lesson for those in authority to hasten wherever they hear of one dead in spirit; Clarke turns it on ministers, who should not think it enough to pray for the sick in their closets. Chrysostom observes that only three disciples went in, Matthew not among them. Read figuratively, Rabanus makes the ruler Moses and the daughter the synagogue in its twelfth year, sick when it should have borne children; Hilary makes him the Law, praying that life be restored to the multitude it raised for Christ.
20:
The disease carried ceremonial uncleanness, which the commentators make the key to her behaviour. Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley cite the Levitical rule and explain her reluctance to apply openly by shame rather than timidity; Clarke declines to describe the complaint further, saying prudence forbids it. Ellicott notices that her twelve years of hope deferred span the ruler's twelve years of joy before his sudden sorrow, and Rabanus builds an allegory on it: she fell sick in the year the girl was born, as the nations turned to idolatry in the age when the synagogue was born among the Patriarchs.

What she touched is described with care. Ellicott reconstructs the dress, the seamless tunic and the loose cloak over it, whose border was probably blue mingled with white, the fringe the scribes wore ostentatiously wide; later tradition, he adds, fixed its threads to represent the six hundred and thirteen precepts. Robertson calls it a tassel of twisted wool at the four corners of the ordinary dress, and remarks that the counting of threads was a refinement he had no concern for. Remigius makes the point devotionally: the Lord wore the hem the Law commanded, and where the Pharisees made theirs large and even worked thorns into some, his was not made to wound but to heal. Jerome observes that she could not meet him in house or town, being shut out by the Law, so she met him on the road, and one woman is cured while he goes to heal another.

Whether her act was faith or something less is argued at length. Calvin is most troubled: he grants she came by the Spirit's guidance but suspects a mixture of sin and error, since her later fear of having offended is opposed to faith, and warns against imitation, since those who copy a remarkable example without God's command are apes rather than imitators, and faith must rest on the word. Robertson concedes an element of superstition while insisting Christ honoured it anyway. Ellicott says the same more gently: she believed the power but not the love, and thought of a physical influence passing from body to garment to hand rather than a will that seeks to bless; yet the germ was accepted, and outward things given a virtue not their own, as the handkerchiefs carried from Paul's body were. Calvin ends where Ellicott does: faith needs forgiveness to please God, and is sustained by fresh help so as to gain strength.

The turning is explained as deliberate. Chrysostom gives four reasons he would not let her slip away: to free her from the fear of having stolen the gift, to correct her supposing she could be hidden, to set her faith before others, and to show he knew all things. Gill adds that the touch could not defile him, the power in him removing her impurity instead, and that the chief purpose was to steady Jairus. Hilary presses the theology: healing reached through the hems because taking a body did not confine a power no body can contain. On the word of dismissal Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott agree that daughter is a tenderness matching the son spoken to the paralytic, and Ellicott presses the verb further, since it says her faith had saved her in the higher sense as well as the lower; Jerome had noticed that it is not shall make thee whole but hath made thee whole, for in believing she was already healed.

One report divides the sources. Ellicott relays from Eusebius that she came from Caesarea Philippi and set up two bronze statues in thanks, one of herself kneeling and one of Christ stretching out his hand, still shown in the fourth century, and that an apocryphal gospel names her Veronica. Lightfoot mentions the same statues at Paneas only to invite the reader to weigh the narrative and judge what the story is worth.
23:
Chrysostom supposes the delay deliberate, that Christ walked slowly and lengthened his talk with the woman so the girl might actually die and the miracle be unmistakable, as he waited three days over Lazarus. Lightfoot cites a rule that even the poorest Israelite owed his dead wife not less than two pipes and one lamenting woman; the crowd gathered suddenly, neighbours out of civility and minstrels perhaps for gain, the more attentive because the parents were of quality. Barnes catalogues the eastern expressions of grief, the women setting up a cry sustained until breath fails and dying away in a sob, hired mourners reciting the virtues of the dead, the violence lasting eight days and a month for a king; Jews, he adds, were forbidden the cutting of flesh practised elsewhere. Wesley notes flutes were used especially for children, louder instruments for adults, and Robertson passes on the unsentimental view that the crowd came for sympathy, for money, and for a share in the meat and drink.

Clarke goes furthest afield, setting the Jewish practice beside an Irish lament he had seen himself: the body laid out and ornamented, mourners divided at head and feet, the chief bard opening in a low doleful tone with the harp, the answering half-chorus taking up the strain from his last note; he had watched two dozen women sing a corpse to the grave-yard. He notes a decree restraining the drinking at such wakes to ten cups apiece, and adds the Roman outcry in which the dead was called by name for eight days, in hope of arresting the departing soul or rousing one merely torpid, until the phrase meaning all is over was pronounced.

The saying that follows is handled with unusual care. Lightfoot observes that calling death sleep was ordinary in the rabbinic writings, so the company would themselves have said the girl slept, which makes it worth asking what form of speech Christ used. Barnes refuses the easy reading: every possible evidence of death had been given, Christ acted on it and meant the people to understand a raising; the word was spoken against their opinion, perhaps a Sadducee one that she had simply ceased to be, and affirms the body dead while implying the spirit lives. Clarke and Wesley take it for a suspension rather than an end. Chrysostom hears reassurance and a lesson not to fear death, since where Christ was present death was only sleep, and insists the restoration brought back the soul that had departed rather than introducing another.

The mockery is turned into evidence. Chrysostom notes that Christ let the derision stand, since the laughter and the pipes together proved she was dead, exactly as he elsewhere let unbelievers convict themselves; and food was ordered for her afterwards so the thing might not be thought a delusion. Gill and Jerome agree the mockers forfeited the sight, Jerome adding that the girl lies dead in the ruler's house still and those who pass for teachers are only minstrels singing dirges. Barnes defends the small audience on evidential grounds: three disciples and the two parents make five impartial witnesses, enough to establish the fact, while more would have turned the room tumultuous, five sober witnesses being better than the confused voices of a rabble.

The mystical readings run alongside. Hilary makes the house the synagogue, where the songs of the Law sounded a strain of wailing. Rabanus moralises instead: the girl is the soul dead in thought, said to sleep because those asleep in sin may still be roused by penitence, and the minstrels are flatterers who cherish the dead; she was raised indoors before a few, the young man outside the gate, and Lazarus before many, since a public scandal requires public expiation. On the spreading report Gill notes that concealment was impossible once neighbours who had known her dead saw her walking and eating.
27:
Chrysostom turns the episode into an indictment: men who had lost their sight believe on hearing alone, while those who could watch the miracles would not. He notes that they did not simply approach but cried out, asking nothing but mercy, and explains Son of David as a title thought honourable, the prophets having used such names for kings they wished to exalt. Henry makes the same contrast, that faith comes by hearing. Jerome turns the title into doctrine and aims it at Marcion and the other heretics who mangle the Old Testament: if he was not born in the flesh, how is he Son of David?

That they were not healed on the road is treated as deliberate. Jerome says they expected a cure in passing and got none until he entered the house, where their faith was proved. Chrysostom offers three reasons: Christ often wished to be asked, so none should think him eager for display; a house was near and healing there private; and their worthiness could be shown, so none might object that if mercy alone saved, all must be saved. Gill and Henry read the silence as a testing of constancy, and we are taught to wait when the answer does not come at the first word.

The question put to them is read as an elevation. Chrysostom observes that he asks not whether they believe he can petition the Father but whether he is able himself, lifting them past the title they had used; answering Lord, they drop Son of David and confess his dominion. Remigius explains the asking of a man who already knew: faith held in the heart and confessed by the mouth earns the higher reward. Calvin enters a caution: knowledge of Christ's power is cold unless we are persuaded of his willingness, since faith embraces the fatherly love along with the strength; he was content with their answer because they had already owned him author of their nation's blessings.

Ellicott marks the touch as the first instance of a method used afterwards with the blind: others had their faith strengthened by the look of sympathy and conscious power in the Healer's face, and being shut out from that, these men needed acts they could connect with the purpose to heal. Calvin draws the general doctrine that prayer in faith is never refused: if two men whose faith was small and imperfectly formed obtained what they asked, the faith of those who have the Spirit of adoption must be more effectual still.

The charge to silence is described in unusually violent terms. Clarke derives the verb from a word meaning to roar or storm with anger; Robertson traces it through its use of horses snorting and men fretting, calls the sense of stern command unknown to older writers, and passes on a gloss that he contracted his brows and shook his head as men do who mean a secret kept; Ellicott hears the panting breath of vehement emotion, as of one seeing garrulous joy about to break out. Whether they were right to disobey divides these sources exactly as Ellicott says it divides commentators, the patristic side approving and the Protestant side not. Chrysostom holds that we should stop those who praise us for ourselves but promote what is said to the Lord's glory; Gregory finds an example in the paradox, that good deeds should be concealed by design and published under compulsion; Jerome says gratitude could not keep quiet. Against them Clarke insists they should have held their peace, since to obey is better than sacrifice, and Calvin calls their haste blameworthy while admitting the reason for the prohibition is unknown, rejecting the suggestion that the ban was meant to provoke more talk. Remigius reads the pair as the two nations, given sight inside a house he takes for the Church; Rabanus makes that house the heavenly Jerusalem.
32:
Remigius admires the sequence, sight given to the blind and then speech to the dumb, reading it off the prophecy that the eyes of the blind shall be opened and the tongue of the dumb loosed; Gill and Clarke press the same text, Clarke treating this cure as demonstrative proof that the Messiah had come.

The affliction is agreed to be no ordinary defect. Chrysostom says the demon's malignity caused it, that the man had to be brought by others because a spirit chained with his tongue left him unable to ask, and that Christ therefore required no faith of him but healed at once. Calvin agrees the possessing spirit had taken away the use of speech, visible signs making it plain the tongue was held bound. Ellicott is more clinical, describing catalepsy or an insanity showing itself in sullen silence, and insisting the dumbness was a spiritual disease rather than a congenital malformation, so the cure restored sanity instead of repairing a body. Robertson notes the word means blunted in the tongue, elsewhere in the ear, and was used of a blunted dart; Jerome observes that common speech favours the sense deaf while Scripture uses it either way. Clarke adds that demons produced paralysis in one host, blindness in another, dumbness in a third, since it served Satan to hide his work as natural disorder.

Ellicott points out that the two responses are set deliberately against each other: the crowd's wonder fell short of faith but was a step toward it, while the Pharisees stood aloof, not denying the facts but supplying their own account. Lightfoot takes the crowd's exclamation to cover the whole day rather than this cure alone, and reconstructs it: dinner with Matthew, the interruption by Jairus, the woman met on the road, the daughter raised, two blind men crying after him and following him home, and a dumb demoniac brought in as they left. Calvin calls the saying hyperbolical, since greater miracles had been done among that people before, but allows the speakers may have had the purpose of the sign in view at a moment when all minds expected the Messiah, and that it was no premeditated judgment but a sudden burst of admiration.

The alternative explanation is attacked from several sides. Chrysostom calls it foolish on its own terms, since demons consent to one another's work rather than fall out, and since Christ also healed lepers, raised the dead and forgave sins, which no demon could or would. Robertson reads it as the desperation of men unable to deny the miracles and reduced to discrediting their author. Calvin warns that wickedness at the height of its blindness will pervert any work of God however plain. Clarke calls it consummate malice to ascribe God's works to the devil, and traces it to envy, which cannot bear approbation given to another; Henry says of the two a dumb devil is better than a blaspheming one, since nothing convinces those under the power of pride. Both Clarke and Robertson note the verse is missing from an old Greek and Latin manuscript and some other witnesses, Robertson judging it genuine nonetheless.

Augustine uses the episode to state a rule of harmony. The story stands in this Gospel only, and the two blind men named elsewhere are not these, as the same evangelist relates both at different points; many acts of the Lord closely resemble each other, so where accounts cannot be reconciled the right inference is that the events were alike and not identical. Read allegorically, Remigius makes the Gentiles the dumb man, unable to open their mouths in confession or made like the mute idols they served; Hilary sees a world diseased in every part; Jerome divides the two responses, the multitude's wonder being the confession of the nations and the Pharisees' scoff the unbelief that lasts to this day.
35:
Ellicott observes that the summary repeats one given earlier almost word for word, and treats it as a second circuit through Galilee introducing the next chapter's discourse; he thinks the two words for illness better rendered the other way about, a distinction the Gloss makes by separating long complaints from lesser infirmities. Jerome notes that preaching came first and healing after, so works might convince those whom words would not. Chrysostom finds in the circuit an answer to the charge just made, since a rebuked demon returns evil for slight while Christ, called an agent of demons, goes on doing good.

Clarke traces the word for compassion to the bowels, taken for the seat of the tender passions; Ellicott finds the phrase so vivid he suspects it preserves Christ's own words about his feeling.

What was wrong with the crowd is genuinely disputed, and the dispute is textual. Barnes builds on the received reading, taking the word for weariness under a burden and describing a people sinking under ignorance and tradition; he fills it out with a land of flocks where the shepherd leads to green pastures and still waters, without whom the sheep stray and pant in the sun not knowing where shade and stream lie. Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson prefer the other reading, which Clarke says the best manuscripts carry and which properly means to pluck out the hair in extreme distress. Ellicott renders it flayed, and thence tormented, insisting they were not sheep merely grown faint but sheep harried by the wolf and preyed on by thieves; Robertson has them rent as if by wild beasts, and takes the second participle for men thrown down prostrate.

That they had no shepherd is taken as an accusation. Wesley points out that teachers were not lacking, scribes being in every city, but none who cared for their souls. Calvin turns it on the priests, scattered through the country to enlighten the people and doing nothing, not one of whom Christ will own as a pastor, and then on his own age, where a crowd under the name of clergy eat up the flock. Remigius makes the contrast the plain one, the good shepherd against the hireling.

The figure then changes. Ellicott notes its first appearance in these three Gospels, later expanded into the parables of the sower and the tares, though the fields seen white among the Samaritans show it was not new. Clarke reports that the rabbins were called reapers and their teaching a harvest, and quotes their saying that the day is short, the work great and the workmen idle. Chrysostom hears Christ quietly claiming to be Lord of the harvest, since the Apostles were sent to reap not another's crop but what he had sown through the Prophets. Remigius dates the increase of labourers to the seventy-two and the descent of the Spirit; Calvin restricts the harvest to the elect mixed among unbelievers, whom God values above the rest of the world.

On the last verse they agree about the verb and divide about its object. Clarke, Wesley and Robertson all press that it means to thrust or drive out, Clarke adding that those fittest are usually most backward and the man eager to preach knows little of his own heart, Wesley that the work is so full of reproach and danger that nature may well shrink from it, and Robertson that God sometimes has to force in a man resisting a known duty. Calvin makes prayer the only remedy for a scarcity of pastors. Ellicott catches what is most human here, that feeling compassion is not enough for Christ, who wants his companions to share it and asks their fellowship in prayer. Gill alone raises the question of address, allowing that the Lord of the harvest may be the Father or Christ himself, in which case the verse witnesses prayer offered to Christ.
